# Kessel schema DSL reference

This reference is generated from the current schema source with the command `make docs` and should not be modified directly.

It's not intended to be a language reference or how-to guide; for those, see the [Kessel docs](https://project-kessel.github.io/docs/start-here/getting-started/).

Symbols are imported from another file by filename (relative to the schema folder) and symbol name. Ex:
```python
load("kessel.star", "resource", "field", "uuid")
```

<a id="builtins"></a>

## Builtins

Predeclared by the interpreter. These need no `load()`.

<a id="builtin-call-ksl-extension"></a>

### `call_ksl_extension`

```python
call_ksl_extension(reporter, name, namespace, **params)
```

Invokes a KSL extension that this interpreter does not generate. Every keyword argument becomes an extension parameter, and the reference is written to the given reporter's namespace.

Do not call this directly from a schema file. Call the thin per-extension wrapper in `extensions/<namespace>.star` instead — see schema/README.md.

<a id="builtin-println"></a>

### `println`

```python
println(*values)
```

Prints its arguments to stdout, for debugging a schema while it compiles. Not part of the schema itself — output goes to the terminal, never to a generated artifact.

<a id="builtin-struct"></a>

### `struct`

```python
struct(**fields)
```

Creates an immutable struct from the given keyword arguments. Fields are read back with attribute access (`s.name`), and the set of field names is fixed at construction. Every DSL constructor in kessel.star returns a struct tagged with a `kind` field.

<a id="module-extensions-hbi-star"></a>

## `extensions/hbi.star`

<a id="extensions-hbi-star-expose-host-permission"></a>

### `expose_host_permission`

```python
expose_host_permission(reporter, v2_perm, host_perm)
```

Exposes an RBAC workspace permission transitively through the host.

**Args:**

- `reporter`: the reporter requesting the permission.
- `v2_perm`: the RBAC permission being exposed.
- `host_perm`: the name it is exposed as on the host type, used with access requests against hosts

**Returns:**

  A function that accesses the workspace permission via a host relation.

<a id="module-extensions-rbac-star"></a>

## `extensions/rbac.star`

<a id="extensions-rbac-star-add-v1-based-permission"></a>

### `add_v1_based_permission`

```python
add_v1_based_permission(reporter, app, resource, verb, v2_perm)
```

Declares a v2 permission derived from an existing RBAC v1 permission.

**Args:**

- `reporter`: the reporter requesting the permission.
- `app`: RBAC v1 application name, taken from the permissions json filename without the .json extension e.g. `"inventory"`.
- `resource`: RBAC v1 resource type, ex: `"hosts"`.
- `verb`: RBAC v1 verb, ex: `"read"`, `"write"`.
- `v2_perm`: name of the v2 permission the v1 one maps onto, ex: `"inventory_host_view"`, used with access requests against the workspace

**Returns:**

  A function that accesses the permission via a workspace relation.

<a id="extensions-rbac-star-add-v1only-permission"></a>

### `add_v1only_permission`

```python
add_v1only_permission(reporter, perm)
```

Declares a permission that exists in RBAC v1, used to create placeholders for permissions for unmigrated services.

Returns nothing

**Args:**

- `reporter`: the reporter requesting the permission
- `perm`: the v1 permission name, constructed from the RBAC application, resource, and verb: {application}_{resource}_{verb}

<a id="extensions-rbac-star-add-contingent-permission"></a>

### `add_contingent_permission`

```python
add_contingent_permission(reporter, first, second, contingent)
```

Declares a workspace permission that depends on two other workspace permissions, commonly used when a permission may be granted anywhere but only applies where it overlaps with another

**Args:**

- `reporter`: the reporter requesting the permission
- `first`: v2 name of the first prerequisite permission
- `second`: v2 name of the second prerequisite permission.
- `contingent`: name of the permission that applies where they overlap, used with access requests against workspaces

**Returns:**

  A function that accesses the combined permission through a workspace relation

<a id="extensions-rbac-star-add-unified-permission"></a>

### `add_unified_permission`

```python
add_unified_permission(reporter, app, resource, verb)
```

Declares a permission whose v1 and v2 names are the same.

The v1 and v2 permission names take the form `{app}_{resource}_{verb}`, and this value is used with access requests against workspaces

**Args:**

- `reporter`: reporter whose namespace the extension reference is written to.
- `app`: RBAC application name.
- `resource`: RBAC resource type.
- `verb`: RBAC verb.

**Returns:**

  A function that accesses the combined permission through a workspace relation

<a id="module-kessel-star"></a>

## `kessel.star`

<a id="kessel-star-resource"></a>

### `resource`

```python
resource(reporter, id_type=None, extends=None, final=False, common={}, fields={}, permissions={})
```

Declares a resource type.

Each resource reported to Kessel must be of a type. A type has fields and permissions.
Fields are the data elements a service reports about a resource. Permissions are like
computed fields that determine which subjects would be allowed to perform an operation.
Permissions can reference a subset of data fields (references to other resources, booleans)
and use set operations to express more complex authorization logic (see Permission expressions below.)

**Args:**

- `reporter`: name of the reporter that reports this resource, e.g. `"hbi"`.
- `id_type`: data type of the resource's identifier. Must be a value data type (not another resource type.) Required unless `extends` is given, in which case the parent's id type is inherited and passing one here is an error.
- `extends`: another resource whose common members, fields, and permissions this resource inherits. An extending resource has no independent identity and must always be associated with an instance of the parent type (reported with the same id.)  Only one level of inheritance is supported, so an extending resource is implicitly final.
- `final`: if true, prevents other resource types from extending this one. This is recommended for types that aren't likely to be part of another service's domain or have no stable identity. Forced to True when `extends` is given.
- `common`: reusable dict of members to add to this type. Types that represent different domain-specific views of the same real-world object (ex: a RHEL VM) can reference the same block of members to have common fields. This is meant for future use with correlation.
- `fields`: dict of member name to declaration. Each member is either a value data field built with `field()` or a relation built with a cardinality function such as `one()`, `many()`, or `boolean()`.
- `permissions`: dict of permission name to a lambda that takes the resource and returns a permission expression, described below. A name starting with an underscore declares an internal member that other permissions in the same type can build on.

Permission expressions:

Each permission lambda receives an object representing the resource being
defined. This object has properties representing the relationship properties of the
type being defined, including common and inherited ones. Relationship properties in turn
have the applicable properties from the types they reference. Sub-properties have no properties-
if deeper nesting is required, there needs to be another permission that continues the chain.
Permissions also have no sub-properties - they must already represent the relevant subject type.

References provide three chaining methods, each returning a new expression
that can be chained again:

- `.union(other)` — subjects from either side have access
- `.intersect(other)` — a subject must appear on both sides to have access
- `.exclude(other)` — a subject has if on the left and not on the right

`any()` and `all()` are helpers for chains of `.union` and `.intersect`
respectively.

```python
workspace = resource("features", extends=rbac_workspace, fields={
    "direct_billing_account": at_most_one(billing_account),
    "ignore_inherited_paid_services": boolean(service),
}, permissions={
    "_paid_services": lambda w: any(
        w.direct_billing_account.services,
        w.parent._paid_services.exclude(w.ignore_inherited_paid_services),
    ),
    "enabled_services": lambda w: w._paid_services.intersect(w._desired_services),
})

Returns:

A resource type object
```

<a id="kessel-star-text"></a>

### `text`

```python
text(minLength=None, maxLength=None, regex=None)
```

A text value data type, optionally length- and pattern-constrained.

**Args:**

- `minLength`: minimum number of characters. There is no lower bound if not specified.
- `maxLength`: maximum number of characters. There is no upper bound if not specified.
- `regex`: pattern the value must match, as a regular expression. It does not apply if not specified. Remember that Starlark strings have no raw-string form, so backslashes must be doubled: `text(regex="^\\d{10}$")`.

<a id="kessel-star-uuid"></a>

### `uuid`

```python
uuid()
```

A UUID value data type.

<a id="kessel-star-numeric-id"></a>

### `numeric_id`

```python
numeric_id(min=None, max=None)
```

An integer identifier value data type, optionally range-constrained.

**Args:**

- `min`: smallest permitted value, inclusive, or None for no lower bound.
- `max`: largest permitted value, inclusive, or None for no upper bound.

<a id="kessel-star-boolean"></a>

### `boolean`

```python
boolean(target=None)
```

A boolean value data type, or a boolean-like relation type.

With no argument this is a true/false data field and not usable in permissions. Given a subject
resource type, it becomes a boolean-like relation, still reported as a true/false value but also
usable in permissions for that subject type.

**Args:**

- `target`: the subject type permissions the value will be used in apply to, or None for a plain boolean data type.

<a id="kessel-star-date-time"></a>

### `date_time`

```python
date_time()
```

A timestamp value data type. Reported as a string in a recognized datetime format.

<a id="kessel-star-enum"></a>

### `enum`

```python
enum(values)
```

A string data type restricted to a fixed set of values.

**Args:**

- `values`: list of permitted strings, in the order they should be published.

<a id="kessel-star-nullable"></a>

### `nullable`

```python
nullable(inner)
```

Permits null in addition to whatever `inner` allows.

**Args:**

- `inner`: the data type to widen. Nesting a `union()` is flattened, so `nullable(union(uuid(), text()))` offers three alternatives rather than a null alongside a nested choice.

<a id="kessel-star-union"></a>

### `union`

```python
union(left, right)
```

A choice between two data types; a value matching either is valid.

Nest calls for more than two alternatives. Note this is specifically for data types.
See `resource` for details on boolean logic in permissions.

**Args:**

- `left`: the first permitted data type.
- `right`: the second permitted data type.

<a id="kessel-star-array"></a>

### `array`

```python
array(items)
```

A list data type whose elements all share one type.

**Args:**

- `items`: the value data type of each element.

<a id="kessel-star-object"></a>

### `object`

```python
object(properties, required=[])
```

A nested structured data type.

**Args:**

- `properties`: dict of property name to data type.
- `required`: list of property names that must be present. Names omitted here are optional.

<a id="kessel-star-field"></a>

### `field`

```python
field(type, required=False, description=None)
```

Declares a data field on a resource, wrapping a value data type.

Relations are declared with a cardinality helper instead and are not wrapped
in `field()`.

**Args:**

- `type`: the field's data type, e.g. `uuid()` or `nullable(text())`.
- `required`: whether a representation must carry this field.
- `description`: documenation for reporters reporting the field.

<a id="kessel-star-self"></a>

### `self`

```python
self()
```

Refers to the resource type currently being defined.

Use it as a relation target so a resource can point at its own type, as in
`at_most_one(self())` for a parent link. Needed because the resource global
does not exist yet while its own `resource()` call is being evaluated.

<a id="kessel-star-wildcard"></a>

### `wildcard`

```python
wildcard(type)
```

A relation to every instance of a type at once.

The reporter supplies a wildcard marker rather than identifiers. Use
`boolean(type)` instead to report the same relation as a true/false flag.

**Args:**

- `type`: the target resource or `self()`.

<a id="kessel-star-at-most-one"></a>

### `at_most_one`

```python
at_most_one(type)
```

An optional relation to a single instance, reported as one identifier.

**Args:**

- `type`: the target resource or `self()`

<a id="kessel-star-one"></a>

### `one`

```python
one(type)
```

A required relation to exactly one instance, reported as one identifier.

**Args:**

- `type`: the target resource or `self()`.

<a id="kessel-star-at-least-one"></a>

### `at_least_one`

```python
at_least_one(type)
```

A required relation to one or more instances, reported as a non-empty list.

**Args:**

- `type`: the target resource or `self()`.

<a id="kessel-star-many"></a>

### `many`

```python
many(type)
```

An optional relation to any number of instances, reported as a list.

**Args:**

- `type`: the target resource or `self()`

<a id="kessel-star-any-of"></a>

### `any_of`

```python
any_of(*types)
```

***Reserved for Future Use***

<a id="kessel-star-any"></a>

### `any`

```python
any(root, *refs)
```

Variadic function that evaluates to true when any of the given permission expressions evaluate to true.

any(a, b, c) behaves the same as a.union(b).union(c)

**Args:**

- `root`: the first expression.
- `*refs`: further expressions.

<a id="kessel-star-all"></a>

### `all`

```python
all(root, *refs)
```

Variadic function that evaluates to true only when all of the given permission evaluate to true.

all(a, b, c) behaves the same as a.intersect(b).intersect(c)

**Args:**

- `root`: the first expression.
- `*refs`: further expressions.
